blocks.text: When a tool finishes running, it has to tell the model what happened. That message is the tool result, and its shape is exactly as important as the tool call that triggered it.
A sloppy result confuses the model just as much as a sloppy answer would confuse a person. A clean result lets the conversation move forward smoothly.
In this topic we will open up the tools call response, look at every kind of content it can carry, and learn how to keep it short and useful.
1. What a Tool Result Actually Is

blocks.alt: What a Tool Result Actually Is
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586530-105054713.png
A tool result is the reply that comes back after the client sends a tools call request and the server actually runs that tool.
It is not free form text. It follows a fixed structure so any client, on any platform, can parse it the same way.
Think of it as a small envelope. Inside that envelope sits the content the tool wants to hand back, plus one flag describing whether things went well.

blocks.title: Why the structure matters
blocks.content: The model never sees your server code. The tool result is the only window it has into what actually happened, so the shape of that window has to be predictable.

blocks.text: 2. The Shape of a tools call Response
Every tools call response follows the JSON RPC envelope, with an id that matches the request and a result object.
Inside that result object there are exactly two fields that matter for this topic, content and isError.
The id lets the client match this reply back to the request it sent. The content array is where the actual payload lives, and isError tells the model how to read that payload.
3. The Content Array
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586530-929620848.png
The content field is always an array, even when there is only one thing to say. That consistency makes parsing much simpler on the client side.
Each item in the array has its own type, and the model handles each type differently.

items: text: plain readable content, the most common case by far
image: base64 encoded picture data, paired with a mimeType
resource: a reference to a file or document, addressed by a uri

blocks.text: You can mix these types freely in one array. A single result might return one short text summary and one image, both in the same response.
4. Text Content
Text content is the workhorse of tool results. Most tools, most of the time, just need to hand back a readable string.
It is a simple object with a type field set to text and a text field holding the actual string.
Because it is plain text, it can carry a sentence, a short report, or even a small chunk of stringified JSON if the caller needs structure.
5. Image Content
Image content lets a tool return a picture instead of, or alongside, words. This is how a screenshot tool or a chart generator sends its output back.
The image bytes are base64 encoded and placed in a data field, with a mimeType telling the client how to decode them.
Models that can see images will read this content the same way they read an image you upload directly in a chat.
6. Resource Content
Sometimes the right answer is not to paste a file into the conversation, but to point at it. That is what resource content is for.
It carries a uri identifying the resource, an optional mimeType, and either inline text or binary data if the client wants to fetch it.
Resource content is a good fit when the underlying file is large and the model only needs a reference plus a small preview.
7. The isError Flag, Tool Failure Versus Protocol Error

blocks.alt: The isError Flag, Tool Failure Versus Protocol Error
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586531-540880738.png
isError answers one narrow question, did the tool itself succeed at its job. It has nothing to do with whether the network call worked.
This is easy to mix up, so it helps to see the two kinds of failure side by side.

blocks.content: {"headers":["","Tool Level Failure, isError true","Protocol Level Error"],"rows":[["Where it lives","Inside a normal successful result object","Replaces the result with a top level error object"],["What it means","The tool ran but the outcome was a failure","The call itself could not be completed"],["Example cause","File not found, invalid input the tool checked itself","Unknown method, malformed request, server crash"],["How the LLM sees it","As content it can read and react to","As a call that essentially never happened"]]}

blocks.text: Compare that to a genuine protocol error, which never even reaches the result field.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.content: isError lives inside a normal, successful response envelope. The call succeeded, the outcome did not.

blocks.text: 8. Returning Multiple Content Items
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586531-695368389.png
A single tool result can hold several content items, and the model will read them in the order you place them.
This is handy when a tool naturally produces more than one kind of output, like a short caption plus a chart.
Order matters here. Put the text that explains the image before the image itself, the same way you would in a written report.
9. How the LLM Consumes a Tool Result

blocks.alt: How the LLM Consumes a Tool Result
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586531-821728100.png
Once the result reaches the model, it gets folded back into the conversation as a new message, tagged as coming from the tool.
The model then reads every content item in order, the same way it reads any other message in the chat history.
Text items become part of its reasoning directly. Image items get processed by its vision pathway if it has one.
After reading the whole array and the isError flag, the model decides what to say next, whether that is a final answer or another tool call.
10. Keeping Results Concise
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586531-452500710.png
A tool result is not a place to prove how much data you collected. It is a place to hand the model exactly what it needs for the next step.
Long, unfiltered dumps waste tokens and often bury the one useful line under noise.

items: Return only what the next step actually needs, not everything you have
Summarize large data instead of pasting it raw
Use isError instead of burying a failure inside a wall of text
Keep image content only when a picture truly adds value
Prefer short structured text over long free form prose

blocks.text: A good habit is to imagine a busy human teammate reading the result over your shoulder. If it would tire them out, it will tire the model out too.
11. Structured Data Inside Text Content
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586532-438811877.png
Sometimes a tool genuinely needs to return structured data, like a small JSON object with a status code and a count.
The MCP content schema does not have a dedicated json type, so the common approach is to stringify it and put it in a text field.
The model can read this like any other text, and many models are quite good at parsing small inline JSON snippets on their own.
12. Common Patterns for Good Results
Good tool results tend to follow a similar shape no matter what the tool does underneath.
Here are patterns worth copying into your own tools.

items: Confirm then summarize, one short line saying what happened
Lead with the answer, keep supporting detail short and optional
Batch related pieces into one text item instead of many tiny ones

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.content: If a person could not skim your result in about five seconds, it is probably too long.

14. Worked Example
Let us walk through a small tool called searchFiles, which looks for files matching a keyword in a project folder.
The client sends a request, and the server responds with a text result listing what it found.
Now imagine the keyword matches nothing at all. The tool did its job correctly, it just found zero results, so isError still stays false.
Only a real failure, like the folder itself being missing, should flip isError to true.
15. Common Mistakes
A few mistakes show up again and again when people first start writing tool results.

items: Returning isError false when the tool actually failed
Dumping an entire database table into one text block
Using a protocol level error for a normal tool failure
Forgetting a mimeType on image content
Returning ten content items when one clear one would do

blocks.text: 16. Practice
Take the broken result below and decide what is wrong with it before reading further.

items: Spot the mismatch: the text clearly describes a failure
Fix it by setting isError to true so the model treats it as one
Rewrite the text so it is short and states only the fact that matters

blocks.text: 17. Key Takeaway
A tool result is a content array plus an isError flag, nothing more mysterious than that. Text, image, and resource items each carry a different kind of payload.
Keep results short, mark real failures with isError, and let a protocol error be reserved for calls that never actually completed. That is most of what good tool results come down to.
